summary: Specifies a format for transporting and provisioning symmetric keys, such as one-time password shared secrets, to cryptographic modules like authentication devices. A common format lets different vendors' components work together.

plainLanguage.summary:
Companies that make authentication tokens have their own file formats for putting a shared secret into a device. This RFC defines one XML format that all of them can use, so a secret can be moved from one vendor's server to another vendor's token.

The container also carries the rules: what the key may be used for, which PIN protects it, and when it stops working.

questions: what is a portable symmetric key container
how are otp keys provisioned to tokens
what does the portable symmetric key container carry
subtitle: An XML container for carrying a shared secret and everything the device needs to use it.

tldr.problem: Vendors of authentication servers and tokens used their own file formats for moving a shared secret into a device, so a token from one vendor could not be loaded by another vendor's server.
tldr.mechanism: PSKC is an XML container for a symmetric key and its metadata: which device and cryptographic module it is for, the algorithm profile, the extra values that algorithm needs, and a policy that says what the key may be used for.
tldr.outcome: Keys can be provisioned between products from different vendors, in bulk, protected by encryption and a digital signature. The document is a Proposed Standard and registers the media type application/pskc+xml.

today: RFC 6030 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It defines the Portable Symmetric Key Container, an XML format for carrying symmetric keys and their metadata, and it registers the media type application/pskc+xml. The algorithm profiles it defines cover HMAC-Based One-Time Password and PIN.

sections.title: Why a Portable Key Container
sections.content:
Symmetric-key systems are used more and more, for example to encrypt data at rest or for strong authentication with One-Time Password (OTP) and Challenge/Response mechanisms. That creates a need for vendors to interoperate and for a standard format for importing and exporting, that is, provisioning, symmetric keys. Vendors of authentication servers and service providers have traditionally used proprietary formats for this, which makes it hard to use tokens from two different vendors.

This document defines a standardised XML-based key container, the Portable Symmetric Key Container (PSKC), for transporting symmetric keys and the metadata that goes with them. It also specifies the information elements that are required when the key is used for a particular purpose, such as the initial counter of the HMAC-Based One-Time Password algorithm. It creates an IANA registry of algorithm profiles, where the algorithm, its metadata and the transmission profile can be recorded in one place for reference.

The version numbering is major.minor, and only version 1.0 is specified. The major and minor numbers are separate integers, each of which may be more than one digit, so PSKC 2.4 is a lower version than PSKC 2.13, which is lower than PSKC 12.3. Leading zeros MUST be ignored by recipients and MUST NOT be sent. The major number is increased only when the message format has changed so much that an older implementation could not interoperate; the minor number marks new capabilities, and it MUST be ignored by an entity with a smaller minor number.
sections.plainLanguage: Companies that make authentication tokens have their own file formats for putting a shared secret into a device. This RFC defines one XML format that all of them can use, so a secret can be moved from one vendor's server to another vendor's token.

sections.title: The Entities of a PSKC Document
sections.content: The container is based on an XML schema and holds six main entities. The KeyContainer entity is the container that carries a number of KeyPackage entities, and a valid container MUST carry at least one KeyPackage. The KeyPackage entity is a package of at most one key together with its related provisioning endpoint or current usage endpoint, such as a physical or virtual device and a specific cryptographic module. DeviceInfo holds the information about the device and the criteria that identify it uniquely. CryptoModuleInfo holds the information about the cryptographic module where the keys live or to which they are provisioned. The Key entity is the key that is transported or provisioned. The Data entity is a list of metadata related to the key, where the element name is the name of the metadata and its value is either encrypted, for example a secret, or in plaintext, for example a counter.
sections.plainLanguage: The document has an outer box that holds one or more packages. Each package holds at most one key, says which device and which cryptographic module it is for, and carries the key together with the extra values the algorithm needs.

sections.title: The KeyContainer and Key Elements
sections.content:
In its most basic form a PSKC document uses the top-level element KeyContainer and a single KeyPackage element. The Version attribute of KeyContainer identifies the version of the schema, this document defines the initial version 1.0, and it MUST be included. The Id attribute carries a unique identifier for the container, which helps when several containers are embedded in a larger XML document.

The Key element has two attributes that MUST be included. Id carries a unique identifier for the symmetric key in the context of key provisioning exchanges between two parties. If PSKC is used in several interactions between the same two parties, with different containers referring to the same keys, the Id of the Key MUST be the same each time, so that a later container can update the metadata of a key that was provisioned earlier. The identifier is a string of alphanumeric characters. The Algorithm attribute contains the identifier of the PSKC algorithm profile, which associates specific meanings with the elements and attributes inside the Key element; this document describes profiles for open standard algorithms, and others are defined in a separate document.

Several optional child elements of Key carry the rest. Issuer names the party that issued the key, for example a bank that issues hardware tokens to its customers. FriendlyName is a human-readable name for the secret key for easier reference; it is informational only, it is a language-dependent string, and it SHOULD carry an xml:lang attribute, with English assumed when that attribute is absent. AlgorithmParameters carries values that influence the result of the computation, such as the response truncation and format in OTP and challenge/response algorithms. Data carries the data about and related to the key.

Inside Data, the Secret element carries the value of the key itself in binary form, the Counter element holds the event counter for event-based one-time password algorithms, the Time element holds the time for time-based ones, and TimeInterval holds the time interval value in seconds for time-based algorithms. The value of a key is encoded as the algorithm profile requires, and the RFC gives separate encodings for AES and Triple DES keys.
sections.plainLanguage: Each key has an identifier and a name for the algorithm that uses it, and it can carry the issuer, a friendly name, algorithm settings and the key value itself. The extra values matter: a one-time password token needs to know the counter it starts at, for example.

sections.title: Key Policy
sections.content:
The Policy element attaches a key usage and a PIN protection policy to a key and its metadata, as a child of the Key element. If the Policy element contains child elements or values that the recipient does not understand, the recipient MUST assume that key usage is not permitted, so that a lack of understanding of an extension cannot lead to unintended use of the key.

The KeyUsage element puts constraints on the intended usage of the key, and the recipient MUST enforce them. The document registers tokens for one-time password generation, challenge and response, data encryption, generating a keyed message digest for integrity or authentication, verifying such a digest, unlocking a device after too many wrong PIN entries, data decryption, key wrapping, key unwrapping, deriving a new key with a key derivation function, and generating a new key from a random number and the previous value. The element may be repeated to express several usages. When it is absent, no constraint is assumed and the key may be used for anything.

The PINPolicy element says how a PIN protects the key. Its PINKeyId attribute gives the identifier of the Key element in the same container that holds the PIN value. The mandatory PINUsageMode attribute says how the PIN is used: Local, where the PIN is checked on the device before the key may be used; Prepend and Append, where the PIN is added to the algorithm response and so must be checked by whoever validates the response; and Algorithmic, where the PIN is part of the algorithm computation. MaxFailedAttempts says how many wrong entries are allowed before the key can no longer be used, with reasonable values of at least 2 and no more than 10. MinLength, MaxLength and PINEncoding describe the PIN itself. A separate element limits how many times the key may be used after it has been received.
sections.plainLanguage: The policy says what the key is for and how the PIN protects it. A receiver that does not understand part of the policy must assume the key may not be used, so an unknown extension cannot lead to the key being used for the wrong thing.

sections.title: Protecting the Key in Transit
sections.content:
Without the EncryptionKey element, information about keys has to be transmitted in cleartext. That element is a child of KeyContainer, and it makes it possible to encrypt keys and associated information. The encryption is applied to the value of individual elements, and the same encryption algorithm MUST be used for all encrypted elements. Three methods are described: encryption based on pre-shared keys, on passphrase-based keys, and on asymmetric keys.

When the algorithm uses an initialization vector, for example AES-128-CBC, a random IV MUST be generated for each value to be encrypted and it MUST be prepended to the encrypted value.

For pre-shared keys, the implementation MUST set the name of the specific pre-shared key in the KeyName element inside the EncryptionKey element, and when the encryption method uses a CBC mode that needs an explicit IV, the IV MUST be passed by prepending it to the encrypted value. The RFC recommends support for AES-128-CBC and for KW-AES128, the key wrap algorithm, and notes that KW-AES128 requires the key being protected to be a multiple of 8 bytes, so for other lengths the key wrap algorithm with padding is recommended.

Since AES-128-CBC does not provide integrity checks, a keyed MAC is applied to the encrypted value using a MAC key and a MAC algorithm declared in the MACMethod element, and the result of the MAC computation goes in the ValueMAC child element of Secret. For the passphrase method, a key derivation function turns the password into the encryption key, the DerivedKey element names the function and its parameters, and the RFC's example uses PBKDF2 with a salt and an iteration count. For the asymmetric method, the recipient's certificate provides the public key that protects the payload.
sections.plainLanguage: The container can encrypt the key it carries. Three ways are described: both sides already share a secret, a person types a password that is turned into a key, or the recipient's public key is used. The encrypted value also carries a MAC, because the cipher on its own does not detect a value that has been altered.

sections.title: Signing the Container
sections.content: PSKC allows a digital signature to be added to the XML document, as a child element of the KeyContainer element. The description of the XML digital signature follows the XML digital signature specification. The example in the RFC shows a signature over a reference to the device, with a canonicalization method, a signature method, a digest method and the digest value, the signature value itself, and the issuer name and serial number of the signing certificate.
sections.plainLanguage: The whole document can be signed, so the receiver can check that it came from the party it expects and that nobody changed it on the way.

sections.title: Bulk Provisioning
sections.content: Bulk provisioning is done by repeating the KeyPackage element several times inside the KeyContainer element, which indicates that several keys are provided to different devices or cryptographic modules. The EncryptionKey element then applies to all of the KeyPackage elements. When several keys are provisioned to the same device, the KeyPackage element is repeated, and the DeviceInfo element inside it carries the same sub-elements that identify that one device, such as the serial number.
sections.plainLanguage: One document can carry many keys for many devices. The container repeats a package for each key, and the encryption set once at the top covers all of them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The container carries sensitive information, such as cryptographic keys, and may be transported from one secure perimeter to another, for example from a provisioning server in a secure room across the Internet to an end-user device attached to a personal computer. Special care MUST therefore be taken over the confidentiality, integrity and authenticity of what it contains.

For confidentiality there are two main approaches. The key data payload may be encrypted, in which case no transport layer security is required, and the usual best practice applies when choosing the strength of the algorithm. A symmetric cipher SHOULD be used, and the longer the key the stronger the protection. Where the sender and the receiver cannot exchange a key encryption key, asymmetric encryption of the payload may be used instead, and again the stronger the key the better. If the payload is encrypted with one of the password-based methods, it may be subjected to dictionary attacks on the password, so strong passwords are needed, and it is strongly RECOMMENDED that implementations use the salt and the iteration count and a different salt value per container. The second approach is to rely on lower-layer security such as TLS or IPsec: the secure connection protects the messages, no payload encryption is needed, and because the plaintext is protected only by the transport layer, the implementation MUST protect against man-in-the-middle attacks, which means authenticating the endpoints of the secure channel.

For integrity, the container offers digital signatures, and it is RECOMMENDED that the signature cover the entire container, so that all the attributes are protected and the integrity of a container can still be checked after it has been delivered.
sections.plainLanguage: The container usually travels across the Internet, so it needs protection of its own or a protected channel. The RFC explains both choices, and warns that a password-based encryption can be attacked by guessing the password.

viz.caption: THE PSKC ELEMENTS AND HOW THEY NEST

root.label: KeyContainer
root.note: Version and Id attributes. Carries at least one KeyPackage.

children.label: KeyPackage
children.note: At most one key, and the device and cryptographic module it belongs to.

children.label: DeviceInfo
children.note: Manufacturer, SerialNo and how to identify the device.

children.label: CryptoModuleInfo
children.note: Which cryptographic module holds the key.

items.label: One-time password
items.desc: The key may only be used to generate one-time passwords.

items.label: Challenge/Response
items.desc: The key may only be used for challenge and response.

items.label: Encrypt
items.desc: The key may only be used to encrypt data.

items.label: Decrypt
items.desc: The key may only be used to decrypt data.

items.label: Integrity
items.desc: The key may only be used to generate a keyed message digest.

items.label: Verify
items.desc: The key may only be used to verify a keyed message digest.

items.label: Unlock
items.desc: The key may only be used for an inverse challenge and response that unlocks a device.

items.label: Key wrap
items.desc: The key may only be used to wrap another key.

items.label: Key unwrap
items.desc: The key may only be used to unwrap another key.

items.label: Derive
items.desc: The key may only be used with a key derivation function.

items.label: Generate
items.desc: The key may only be used to generate a new key from a random number.

viz.caption: THE THREE WAYS TO PROTECT THE KEY

cells: A secret both sides already hold
Its name goes in the KeyName element, and a keyed MAC covers the encrypted value.
A key derivation function turns the password into a key. Use a salt and an iteration count.
Used when the two sides cannot exchange a key encryption key first.

items.title: Confidentiality
items.text: Encrypt the key payload, or carry the container over a protected channel.

items.title: Integrity
items.text: Sign the container, preferably covering all of it.

items.title: Authenticity
items.text: Check who signed it, and keep the channel endpoints authenticated.
